utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. We meet in most cases for the first time. I would ask the registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, good afternoon. The case number IT-04-82-PT, the Prosecutor versus Boskoski and Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I take it that each of the accused can hear what is now being said in a language they understand? I expect Macedonian. I see both nodding agreement. Thank you. Could I ask first for appearances for the Prosecutor. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, Your Honour, with my colleagues, Mr. Anees Ahmed and Ms. Angel Langenberg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Now, for Mr. Boskoski. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am the Defence counsel of Mr. Boskoski and together with Mr. Guenael Mettraux, Dragan Godzo and Jesenka Residovic who is the legal assistant and case manager of our team. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. And for Mr. Tarculovski. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the accused Tarculovski, the counsel Antonio Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure that all will be aware of the order of the 23rd of November appointing me as the Pre-Trial Judge in this matter together with two of the Judges who previously formed the Trial Chamber, and we come together today I believe for the fifth Status Conference. The object of a Status Conference, if I could remind those here, especially the accused, is to organise the pre-trial exchanges between the parties, if organisation is needed; to ensure the speedy preparation for trial; and to allow issues to be raised by any parties, especially the accused, relating to matters of concern; and also to enable the accused to raise matters concerning their mental or physical condition, if there are any such issues. Now, there are items that have been noted down as requiring either mention or further submission or attention. The first of those is the matter of Defence counsel. The position, if I could ask you, Ms. Residovic, in respect of assistant counsel, are you in a position to tell me at what stage you are at there?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already put forward the name of Mr. Guenael Mettraux for co-counsel; we made that proposal to the Registry. At the moment, we are awaiting the decision by the Registry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. There may be a possibility for Mr. Mettraux to supplement the information before the Registry as to his formal qualification, either as professor or as a practising lawyer to overcome some uncertainty. That may be something that could usefully be discussed with the Registry before you leave The Hague now. I'm sure if further assistance could be given, it could speed up the decision process.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We are going to do so today and we'll provide all the additional necessary documents following this Status Conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, for Mr. Boskoski, Mr. Apostolski, it's not clear what position you have reached with respect to assistant counsel. Could you help me there, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have proposed a co-counsel, Pavce Neftenov, who has been by the Registry required to pass an additional exam for the knowledge of foreign language and at this moment, that's the status of this matter and we are negotiating with several other colleagues that fulfill the requirements to be co-counsels and during the month of January we will be able to appoint a co-counsel, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I take it from that, then, that neither Defence teams see the issue of co-counsel as one that will provide any impediment to the trial getting underway during the first half of next year. The next issue is that of translation of materials and language of trial. I think -- I believe I come back to you again, Ms. Residovic, with respect to language at trial firstly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we've already raised that issue during the last Status Conference and the Judge told us, invited us to continue our discussions with the Registry and encouraged us to try and find a solution that would comply with the rights of my client and that would also meet the requirements, the technical requirements here at the Tribunal. We've already had discussion with Ms. Nikolic who is the head of the interpretation unit. We also had a discussion with the head of OLAD and with the Deputy Registrar yesterday, and we wrote a letter listing our main arguments relating to this matter. They are as follows: First of all, our client speaks two languages, his mother tongues, he has a dual nationality, in other words, he chose counsel that speaks his own language, that is to say, one of his mother tongues. My client is from Macedonia, he speaks Macedonian, of course, but he's also a Croatian citizen and speaks B/C/S. And for that reason, I believe that if you look at Article 21 of the Statute, he has the right to have counsel that speaks his own language because it is stated in this article that he is entitled to receive a translation of what is said by anybody in the courtroom who doesn't speak his own language. But I'm his counsel. I speak his language, and therefore, it is not necessary for anyone to translate what I say to him. It's a right that he has, and it's a right that has been invoked in previous cases before the Tribunal. Mr. Aleksovski also was of Macedonian origin. The case was closed many years ago and Croat was used in his case before the Tribunal therefore the case is not new. Furthermore, we stated in the letter to the Deputy Registrar that when I use my own tongue, my own mother tongue, my own language, I can be more specific when I ask questions and when I make comments. I can communicate better with all the witnesses and with all those present in the courtroom and this could enable the trial to go faster and this could be a way to speed up the proceedings once the trial starts. This will in no way cause a burden to the budget of the Tribunal and -- but since this question is -- this matter is still under discussion, I believe that we'll inform you as soon as we've reached a solution with the Registry. Of course, if there's a problem, we'll file a motion with the Chamber to ask the Chamber to rule on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have given a written submission now to the Registry, have you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wrote a letter to the Registry and we are waiting for the decision by the Registry. I don't think that this is going to make any problems because once, when I spoke with Ms. Nikolic about the matter, she said that we can find a solution to technical problems quite easily, and it doesn't need to cost a lot of money either. Let me give you an explanation about this. I understand the Macedonian language rather well. It's a passive language for me. I can understand also the English when I read it on the screen, and I can also understand French. Therefore, the only thing we need here is for B/C/S to be translated from -- into English or into French, but when other people speak Macedonian or English or French, none of this need to be translated into B/C/S for my benefit. The only thing that we need is for me, when I speak B/C/S, there needs to be a translation of what I say into English or into French. That's the only problem that needs to be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You seem to have a considerable facility in French, if I might respectfully say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. But of course when you speak your mother tongue, you can speak faster and better than when you speak a foreign language. But first of all here, we are not talking only about my right and my obligations, we have to think of the rights of accused who need to be able to listen to me in his own language and thus he will not need to wait for what I say in French to be translated into Macedonian or into Croatian. Therefore, when I speak to the witnesses, to the Judges, or to anyone else, then if I speak in B/C/S, then you will be able to understand me immediately without interpreters having to translate what I say. Furthermore, this could have another consequence because everyone in Macedonia, even the Macedonians or the Albanians, those who can listen to us on the Internet or otherwise, those who can listen to the proceedings will be able to understand me because in Macedonia and in all the other countries of the former Yugoslavia, everybody can understand B/C/S, everybody can understand me, and doesn't need any translation of what I say in their mother tongues. So if we take that solution, this would have a further impact and would further the idea of a speedy and fair trial more so than if I were to speak French in this -- in these proceedings. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you. The matter presently is before the Registrar. I haven't had to sit down and worry through the issue myself yet, but I just comment that I wonder whether you are not sliding together two separate issues when you say the right of the accused to have counsel of choice and right of the accused to hear his counsel in his own language. He has a right to be able to hear in his mother tongue or to have a translation into his mother tongue. Your submissions do seem to obscure that difference but for me at the moment, I don't have to worry about that, that can wait. The Registrar will be dealing with it and clearly you now have put your position to the Registrar and we will await his decision shortly. One way or another, it's clear that it will be necessary for, either by interpretation or otherwise, the accused to be aware of what occurs in the proceedings and for you to be able to conduct your case. I'm sure that will be managed in some useful way. Thank you on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the translation of documents, perhaps I could ask you, Mr. Saxon, do you see any such issues presenting difficulty in the final stages of preparation of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on what the parties were informed yesterday, that the Chamber is planning on starting this trial either in the end of March or in the beginning of April, at this moment, the Prosecution does not foresee a problem. We are still awaiting the translation from Macedonian to English of several hundred pages of documents that were originally in the Macedonian language. They are now with the representatives of CLSS; however, CLSS has told us that this work should be complete by the end of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there documents that you have provided that have to be translated into Macedonian, 68 ter documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I didn't hear the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Rule 68 disclosure documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not -- it's never been the Prosecution's understanding that under Rule 68, we have an obligation to translate materials into Macedonian and quite frankly, we have not been translating materials disclosed under Rule 68 into the language of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was confused, I've got to say, by a comment made to me following yesterday's proceedings about that. I think it's a comment that was made by one of the Defence counsel, and it implied to me that you were translating. Maybe he was indicating that their process of translation is taking time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was my understanding yesterday, Your Honour, from a comment made by one of my learned colleagues that their review and translation of some of the material which the Prosecution has disclosed to the Defence under Rule 68 is taking some time. Yes. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. So from your point of view, your obligations can be met certainly by March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do either Defence teams see any difficulty with the process of translation of materials necessary for trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We mentioned yesterday during the 65 ter Conference that CLSS informed us, once again, on the 6th of December that they have limited capacities for translation of documents from Macedonian into English and this is a concern for us. We are concerned because we have a lot of documents to translate, first documents which we have found during our investigations and also those very important documents which the Prosecution conveyed to us through -- disclosed to us through Rule 68 and it was also mentioned that only 100 pages are translated per month and this is a bit dangerous for the preparation of the Defence case, all the more so as among the documents we have received from the Prosecution through Rule 68, we have documents which are in Albanian and in German, of course those are not the documents which will be used during the trial and these are not languages of the accused or counsel, but this means that we will have to ask from CLSS a translation from these documents because we don't even know whether these documents are really pertinent or are really -- may be used really as exhibits, exculpatory exhibits. Another matter which we would like to request, Your Honour, is that could you encourage or request from the Registry that he may ask the CLSS to give a priority to all these documents which come from Defence, because this will enable us to be better prepared for the beginning of the trial. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With respect to your last request, as I understand the matter, the interpretation unit is gathering together its Macedonian resources for this trial and that, naturally, is a process that takes time and their capacities at the moment are somewhat limited. So I think there is little point in making some sort of grand order that is beyond realistic capacity to deliver. From what I understand, the work is being dealt with as expeditiously as possible at the moment, but what it means is we need to be sure that it is completed before the trial starts so that you've had an opportunity to familiarise yourself with it by that time. So thank you for that. Is there anything affecting the preparation of your case, Mr. Apostolski, in this question of the translation of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as has been presented by my learned colleague Residovic, we do have some hundred documents which are going to be given to CLSS for translation and I would like to inform this Court that a large number of the documents we have provided our own translation and we will try to provide, on our own resources, to provide translation of these documents as much as we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next issue is one of disclosure. Is there any aspect of that, Mr. Saxon, that you see is yet to be completed and which may present a problem for a commencement of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There are no aspects of disclosure which, in the Prosecution's submission, will affect the commencement of the trial. There will be one additional witness statement disclosed this week pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii). And I need to inform the Chamber and the parties of one other matter. As you can imagine, it's difficult for a Prosecutor to acknowledge that a Defence counsel was correct on a particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Never, never, Mr. Saxon. Defence counsel are very often correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know they are, and yesterday one of them was correct on a point in our meeting and I have to acknowledge that. Ms. Residovic politely suggested that the Prosecution undertake another review of its files to make sure it had no other witness statements that it needed to disclose and this morning I discovered that there is one remaining statement that the Prosecution will disclose today, not under Rule 66(ii), not under Rule 68, but under Rule 66(B), Your Honour. This is pursuant to a request that the counsel for the accused Boskoski made one year ago today of disclosure of all witness statements taken by the Prosecution in this case. That request was made pursuant to Rule 68 but the Prosecution told the parties that it would take that request or interpret that request as a request under Rule 66(B) and this is one more statement that was taken recently. It was given by a person who will not be called by the Prosecution as a witness however, we do feel it falls under Rule 66(B) and we will disclose it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Perhaps I could start with Mr. Apostolski for a change. Is there any disclosure matter that is causing you concern at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dear Judge, I believe that on the part of the Prosecution, they have been -- had a proper attitude and they are not disclosing more of the evidence but I hope that in that direction -- so on our part there is no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Ms. Residovic, do you have any difficulty with disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My perusing all the documents which the Prosecutor disclosed to us up to now by Rule 66 or Rule 68, certain problems were mentioned yesterday during the Conference 65 ter. Here we wish to say only that we are -- keep strictly all the documents which the Prosecution disclosed to us. For the list of exhibits and all the exhibits of the Prosecution, we are going to propose certain decisions to the Chamber to see that the possibility is given to have a fair trial. We have found several scores of documents which do not correspond to the case and we are therefore preparing proposals on this matter. As for the exhibits, exculpatory exhibits which the Prosecution disclosed according to Rule 68 mentioned yesterday, we said yesterday that we think, by looking at all these documents, that the Prosecution has not sufficiently reviewed these documents and disclosed documents which put us in a position which we have to do his job. We have more than 30.000 pages to review and being fully responsible for this, we are going to disclose this to the Prosecution and if it becomes necessary, also to the Judges. So this is the position we find ourselves in today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, where does that leave us? I'm not quite sure what you were saying about the commencement of the trial. Is this going to present a problem for a commencement in March or April?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Everything will be ready. Our proposal will be ready within a month and we are sure that all these problems may be solved before that, and we will be ready for trial with the dates which have been mentioned yesterday during the 65 ter Conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May the Prosecution respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one point, perhaps, to try to try to make this process more efficient. For the past year, the Prosecution has put the Defence on notice that we were searching our evidentiary collections, initially on 148 different search criteria to identify material falling within the scope of Rule 68 for this case. Subsequently, we added three more criteria, so the final -- the final number -- excuse me, we began with 145 criteria. The number now is 148. As I explained yesterday, the Prosecution is initiating updated searches to make sure there is not additional material that might assist the accused in the preparation of their Defence that has come into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor since our last process, which ended about ten months ago. It might be helpful for the Defence to review these search criteria once more and inform the Prosecution whether they now feel that some of these search criteria are no longer necessary, because if that were the case, that would certainly reduce the time and effort spent by the Prosecution on this exercise and would certainly reduce the amount of material subsequently disclosed to the Defence under Rule 68. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I would simply ask that Defence counsel give that consideration and if it were possible, to limit the possible search fields. You will understand that would A, speed up the process of searching, but more importantly, lessen the amount of no longer relevant material that you would have to spend time on in your own preparation. So it would assist your own work if there were some issues that you were happy to put aside altogether in the search criteria presently being pursued by the Prosecutor. I turn now to the -- Ms. Residovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour, we accept this suggestion and we will look into the research criteria which are necessary, but we have to do our duty and we have to be absolutely sure that we do things correctly and we prepare the Defence of our client in a fair way. But for this matter, once again, I have another question which was mentioned yesterday and which I also mentioned during the last Status Conference when we asked the Prosecution to inform us whether he had finished the investigations in our case. Last time, the Prosecution said very clearly, in front of Judge Zanetta [as interpreted] and the last letter which was sent on the 8th of December, he told us as he did yesterday, during the conference yesterday, that the investigations were continuing. So this means that we can't know very clearly today what is the situation of the Prosecutor. Therefore, we are not really in a position to prepare in the necessary way for the counsel who are responsible for the defence of their client. Therefore, I am telling you that the Defence is very surprised because on several occasions, the Prosecution told us that the investigations were going on and the Security Council in its Resolution 1503 and the Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte mentioned several times in her reports to the Security Council that investigations were over in 2004. This is the reason why we would like to know really when the Prosecution will stop these investigations and will communicate disclosed new documents which have been found in these investigations after the confirmation of the indictment. And, on the other hand, we are now in a position to tell you that the way we understand our case is what we have said in our pre-trial brief and we are going to prepare our defence this way. And we are going to suppose [as interpreted] that each time the Prosecutor will request or try to change, to alter the indictment or the case or its case, or changing certain words or any -- in any other way, this is something which -- this is a situation which is very difficult for the Defence because we must know what is the case of the Prosecution. Now, here, there is a mistake in the transcript, line 14, going to oppose, we will oppose, not suppose, each time -- each time there will be a request to alter the case. It's very clear that such situations -- it's very important for our understanding, even of the duration of the case, not only for the rights of the accused, not only to know exactly what the case is and how it stands today, but also to know what will be the duration of the case once it has started. And another matter about this situation, we are also expecting the decision of the Appeal Chamber to see exactly what the case is, this is very important for the Defence to know what are the measures which has to be taken to prepare for the beginning of the case -- or the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I indicate that the Chamber is aware of the pending Appeal Chamber decision raising particular matters of jurisdiction and naturally we expect that decision to have been delivered well before the trial commences and proceedings in the trial will be in light of that decision. On the former matter, Mr. Saxon, do you want to put any submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you will allow me, yes, Your Honour, very briefly. Your Honour, it is the Prosecution's submission that post-indictment investigations by the Prosecution are the absolute norm in this Tribunal. They have occurred on every trial that I have been involved with and I believe they have occurred on every trial that my learned colleague Ms. Residovic has been involved in going back to the Celebici case. Ms. Residovic mentioned Security Council Resolution 1503. A careful reading of that resolution, Your Honour, indicates that what the Security Council was referring to in one clause where it said, "It calls on the ICTY to take all possible measures to complete investigations by the end of 2004." In that clause, it was referring to pre-indictment investigations. It was not referring to, Your Honour, any further post-indictment work on factual and legal issues related to the Prosecution's case. Certainly, the Defence has not provided any authority to the contrary. The Prosecution would respectfully direct the Chamber and the parties to a decision of this Trial Chamber in Prosecutor versus Cermak and Markac, case number IT-03-73, from the 19th of October, 2005, paragraph 51 in which this Trial Chamber said: "The Chamber accepts the Prosecution's submission that it may properly conduct ongoing investigations against an accused after an indictment has been confirmed." Indeed, Your Honour, Rule 2 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence define investigations as "activities undertaken by the Prosecutor whether before or after an indictment is confirmed." That Rule certainly was not changed after UN Security Council 1503 or the finalisation of the Prosecution's indictments in the end of 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate, Ms. Residovic, I don't believe there's need for any further submission. I well understand the proposition you are putting. The Security Council resolution to which you refer has generally been understood and applied in this Tribunal as referring to those investigations that lead to the institution of proceedings, that is, that lead to the filing of an indictment to commence proceedings. Although a similar style of language is used, there is a distinct process that is undertaken in the course of a trial and that is a process of ensuring that the information presented to the Chamber is correct at the time of its presentation, and it may well be that further inquiries prompted by the course of the proceedings, what witnesses have said or issues that are being raised by other counsel, will lead to the identification of some additional witness or some additional point of issue. When that occurs, it is necessary for the party, whether it be Prosecution or Defence, that want to introduce something that is not part of their pre-trial brief and disclosure - and this is especially so for the Prosecution - it is necessary for that party to satisfy the Trial Chamber that it is in the interests of justice that they be allowed to introduce that additional material so that the trial proceeds at this point on the basis of the case disclosed to the Defence in the pre-trial brief and the disclosed material. Should the Prosecution wish to vary that in some way by the addition of a witness or an issue, or some amendment to the terms of the indictment, the Prosecution must first satisfy the Trial Chamber that it should have leave to do so and at that point, the consequences for the Defence of introducing fresh material or some amendment to the indictment is considered by the Trial Chamber and a decision is made whether or not it is fair. It is in the interests of justice that that be allowed. If it is allowed, there may be consequences for the Defence. You may need to, yourself, then, investigate this additional issue. You may have to look at the consequences of an amendment to the indictment, and the Trial Chamber on application by the Defence will consider whether you should have additional time to do that, what opportunity you need to be given as a matter of fairness to enable you to prepare to meet this new element, and that way, the trial is kept fair even though there may be some change. I would just add that, somewhat as a novelty in this Tribunal, this is expected to be quite a short trial. If a trial has gone on for two years or maybe four years, there is quite a scope for change occurring. If we are looking at a short trial, the scope for that is obviously much more limited so that it's not likely, I would think, to be an issue that will produce any great problem for the ongoing conduct of the Defence case in a trial of this size. I think what all parties recognise, and certainly it is the view of the Trial Chamber in this case, the interests of both accused are best met by getting this trial heard and determined as quickly as can be, having given everybody a fair opportunity to present their case. And that will be guiding the Trial Chamber in the conduct of the case. But for the reasons I've indicated, some new point or points may arise in the course of the Prosecution case. They must first satisfy the Trial Chamber, having heard you, that they should be allowed to do so before the case can proceed on the basis of the new information. Does that assist you to feel a little more comfortable about the fact that you may not know, at this moment, every possibility that could occur in the course of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've understood your comments, thank you very much. But Mr. Saxon mentioned one thing and let me -- allow me please to say two things. In this case, the investigation has been going on since 2001 and went on from 2001 to the confirmation of the indictment. And as for the sources, Mr. Saxon said that I did not mention any authorities, any sources. Let me say that in my letter to the President of the Tribunal from 31st of May, 2006, or rather in his letter to the Security Council on the 31st of May, 2006, the President of the Tribunal, Mr. Pocar, stated very clearly that all the investigations had been completed and in the report of Ms. Del Ponte dealing with the situation in the Republic of Macedonia, it is stated in -- and these are official documents, that the Prosecutor has completed all investigations related to that country. Four cases are also mentioned that were referred to the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor stated that all had been completed. This is the third case where I'm going to work as a Defence counsel and I fully understand your comments, Your Honour, but still, the Security Council has set some limits to the work of the Prosecution and when I worked in the Hadzihasanovic and Celebici, this resolution had not been passed at the time. Thank you for allowing me to speak about the matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Ms. Residovic. I don't think what you have put would cause me to change anything that I have indicated. Investigations leading to new indictments were closed pursuant to the resolution and as reported to the Security Council. But, for example, it is a right of an accused to be, right up to the end of the close of the case and decision, to be informed of any exculpatory material that should come to light in the hands of the Prosecutor. That often is a product of ongoing investigation, if you can properly call it that, into the case being tried. So it is a matter that is in as much in the interests of Defence as Prosecution that if new material that's important in the case comes to light, the Prosecution has an obligation to disclose it and if it wants to rely on it, it must then come to the Chamber which will hear the Defence to see whether that should be allowed. The process of agreement of facts I know is ongoing. Do you expect there will be any significant further progress in that field, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I hate to use the word "expect," Your Honour, however, I am always hopeful and optimistic, and the Prosecution has a meeting scheduled with Defence counsel for Mr. Tarculovski to discuss this matter later today and we also hope to be able to continue these discussions with our friends, the counsel for Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. I don't think I should pry into the approaches being taken by Defence counsel at this point. I would merely encourage both Defence counsel in the interests of an efficient and speedy resolution of the case to look with fairness at the question of agreement of facts. The Chamber is aware that there are now a number of motions that are awaiting decision, and they are in the course of consideration at the moment, and they should be dealt with very early in the new year. You should get your decisions in all of those matters, including the question of expert reports, and the 69 or so Rule 92 bis statements that are the subject of motions. The timing of the trial, you've heard our expectation that it might be possible to commence the trial at the end of March or in the first half of April. One or two things said today, especially by Ms. Residovic would suggest to me that it might be better into April than at the very end of March; just a little more time might be useful. I would also, in frankness, indicate to you that the present trial this Chamber is conducting will conclude in the first week of March. It's a trial that's gone for well over a year and a decision has to be prepared. So that we will be under tight time pressure during March, and I expect into April, in preparing that decision. I also noticed today that we encounter Easter at the end of the first week of April so that putting those things together, it may be that we should commence after Easter rather than get the case interrupted by a holiday very early on in the beginning. If there are no further submissions indicating difficulty with a commencement in the course of the first half of April, I will simply move on from there and a programming order will be made in due course which fixes a firm starting date. But I understand from yesterday that no counsel then saw any insurmountable problem to commencement in the first half of April. Is that correct? Well, you can expect that that will be the time indication given when an order is delivered. I think there's little point at the moment in going over again the question of how long the trial can be anticipated. You've each given fairly -- well, certainly the Prosecution has given detailed indications. The Defence seeks to know more, perhaps, about the case against it before reaching any final view. Certainly it's appreciated that the motions concerning 92 bis statements will affect the length of the hearing, but we seem to be looking at a quite short trial, by the normal standards in this Tribunal. I commend counsel for their efforts to try and ensure that and I can assure you that the Trial Chamber will approach the matter with a view to dealing with the trial as efficiently and quickly as fairness will allow. Now, I should turn to each of the accused to ask, firstly of you, Mr. Boskoski, whether there is any matter of health or any concern you have about the condition of detention. I ask you directly. You may prefer to have your counsel reply but I just ask you directly so that you know you may speak if you wish. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the outset, I would like to ask from you an apology because the answer at the very beginning with yes or no was demonstrated by a vertical nodding of the head by which we have confirmed that we do understand that everything is fine and all right with regard to the translation. I believe and I hope that you will accept this apology because there is a country in the neighbourhood where the nodding of head means no. That's Bulgaria. However, I would like to indicate that my health condition is better, as you can see. I am well, and pleasantly in a good mood. I believe the conditions in the detention unit are very good and decent. The control is okay, and I do not have any specific objections. My health condition, my mental and my physical condition are all right, and I -- I believe I will retain such a condition. If you would allow me, I would like to express my gratitude to the Prosecution in order to prove our innocence by giving us additional materials and documents which will be exculpatory in non-existence [as interpreted] of the accusations. My thanks again to them and to you, Your Honour, and to the staff of the court and let me wish you a Christmas and good Christmas season and New Year's Day to the Prosecution staff and to the Prosecution itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boskoski. Mr. Tarculovski, do you have any concerns that you wish to raise about the matters I've indicated? THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Everything is fine. My health is okay. Everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I just encourage the accused to keep fit and that will help us in the process of the trial. Yes. Thank you very much. I see, Mr. Saxon, that you have a motion for the admission of exhibits. It's a long, and it's an old motion, 7th of November, 2005. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to be honest, it does not, but -- the 7th of November, 2005 is some time ago but I will certainly take your word for it. I've been reminded gratefully by my colleague as to the substance of this motion. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Could I indicate that as a matter of procedure, the -- if there are matters that are not objected to, just as if there are facts which are agreed between the parties, the Trial Chamber would expect at the opening of the trial that those would be noted. The exhibits received and a document recording the agreed facts would be then received as an exhibit and marked as such, so that there is a complete record in the trial process itself. So if you could prepare on that basis. I see that there remain still quite a number of exhibits which are the subject of a debate and discussion between you and that list of matters that are not objected to may well get longer in the time between now and the commencement of the trial. But I just let you know, as a matter of procedure, that would appear to the Trial Chamber the most convenient way of dealing with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, and if we make further progress also regarding agreements on the admission of exhibits, we would also produce a similar document then regarding such exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. There are no other matters that I would think need to be raised here. Do you see anything else, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, with your leave if we might go into private session for one brief moment. It's a matter related to a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, any further matter that you would wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Merci. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Court to issue an order that it would be allowed to the Defence of Mr. Johan Tarculovski so that our response on the filings of 92 ter be prolonged for another seven days given that it's about a very comprehensive material and the Defence of Johan Tarculovski's completely here in The Hague, it's preparing for a week already for the trial both and also for the -- our readiness for our presentation to the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're seeking an extension of time to comply with that until Wednesday the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. By Wednesday, 20th, it will be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, any submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I've never been good at mathematics as my colleagues can attest. I think-- I believe that these responses would be due normally on the 20th, so if my colleague is seeking a one-week extension, he's seeking an extension until Wednesday the 27th of December, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I misunderstood. I thought a week further from today was being sought. When is it that you will be in a position to file, on the 20th or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not good with mathematics. I think that it we will be able to respond by the 27th of December, Wednesday, so I have mixed up the dates, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how many people will be in the Office of the Prosecutor to receive them on the 27th, but you may have until the 27th of December to complete your work and file and -- are you filing electronically?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, in electronic form, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could file and send it electronically to the Prosecutor, that would be a good idea. Well, if there is no other matter, we will close this Status Conference. I would return the compliment of Mr. Boskoski and wish all parties the compliments for Christmas and we look forward to seeing more of you in the new year.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
